newsitem.title: UK: Lira's post ERM entry rally will not last - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Lira's post ERM entry rally will not last - analysts.

text.p: The lira rallied half a percent in immediate reaction to the announcement late on Sunday that it had re-joined the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) but analysts doubt the firmer tone will last long.

After 17 hours of talks at the weekend EU ministers finally agreed on a central rate of 990 per mark for the lira, and it subsequent gravitation towards the central rate took it from 999.00 to around 994.00 per mark.
Its 15 percent limits are 1,149.56 and 852.59 but Italy is likely to attempt to shadow 2.25 percent limits at around 1013.00 and 968.00, analysts said.
"The argument for buying lira now they have joined is a little tenuous," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas.

He noted that after Finland joined the ERM last month at a central rate of 3.04 markka per mark, the mark/markka cross moved from 3.01 to 2.9950, half a percent. It is currently trading back around the 3.01 per mark level.
"The whole rally in the markka after joining was half a percent and the post-ERM rally lasted less than a month, it would be amazing if Italy lasted longer," Parsons said.
"I hate to trot out it out again but it is a case of...Buy the mystery, sell the history."

The fact that ERM membership is not a rubber-stamp for inclusion in a single currency in 1999 and the fact that Italy must cut interest to meet optimistic growth and fiscal targets both point to an easier lira, say analysts.
Many expect a cut in Italy's 7.5 percent official discount rate soon, maybe as early at the end of this week, given recent weak inflation data.
Other member states were quick to point out that Italy's inclusion in the ERM was not an automatic key to EMU.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said Italy's return to the ERM was not a "prejudicial decision."
"It is certainly not a comment on Italy's qualification for monetary union," Tietmeyer warned.

"In the short term the move will give Italian asset markets and the lira a boost but longer term this view may begin to be doubted as the main obstacles to EMU membership remain in place," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
He said once the initial euphoria is out of the way the risks on the lira are more to the downside.

"You can't rule out another little spate of buying just to take it to the central rate but one huge reason to be long of lira has been removed," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"There are no good reasons for taking the lira into the firmer half its band for long, there is simply no justification for it," he added.
Analysts said there was a chance that the market could test the Italian authorities in the very near-term by gently pushing the lira up until the Bank of Italy intervened to rein it in.
"They may keep nudging the bear just to see when it wakes up," one said. "But that sort of game won't last long."
At 1000 GMT on Monday the lira had got to within a whisker of its new central rate at 990.15 per mark.
